faq.q: What do these clothing ad templates include?
faq.a: You get the olive bomber on an AI avatar, a spoken line, and a file you can approve. A flat-lay photo is enough to start, with no model booking.

faq.q: How does a clothing template become an ad?
faq.a: Upload the bomber photo and name the shopper, such as someone buying a lighter layer. The draft comes back as an on-model file you can post. Your shop software can send that photo for you.

faq.q: Which kinds of clothing can I start with?
faq.a: Start with the olive bomber, a dress, or a tailored trouser. Streetwear, activewear, and occasion pieces fit when a person can wear them. A folded stack is a weak source photo.

faq.q: Can I make several ads for one collection?
faq.a: Yes. The same bomber can run once for a commute and again for a wet weekend, using the photo you already have. A second language can be its own file.

faq.q: Which shops are these clothing templates built around?
faq.a: A shop that sells its own jackets and restocks through the month. The owner can run it, or someone on the marketing desk can. An agency can repeat the path for each clothing client.

faq.q: Can I use them if I have never edited a video?
faq.a: Yes. You supply the bomber and say what the ad should show. The template handles the avatar, the opening, and the cut. Earlier video experience is not required.

faq.q: After I upload a garment, when is the ad ready to post?
faq.a: The on-model file is ready to download once generation finishes. Take it and post the cut the shop already uses. Lengths for a clip are 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds.

faq.q: What does a clothing ad cost, and can I post the square crop?
faq.a: A 6-second clip spends 24 credits, 10 seconds spends 40, 15 seconds spends 60, and 30 seconds spends 120. A still of the same bomber spends 24 credits. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, Pro is $35 for 300, and Premium is $63 for 600. The screen shows that cost before you start. Notes on the square crop are on [AI Instagram ads](page:plat-instagram).

reviews.h2: Shops Switching to AI On-Model Photos
reviews.lead: Example ways a clothing shop uses one garment photo. These cards are not customer quotes.

items.t: New jacket on the product page
items.d: The shop uploads the hanger photo when the carton arrives and places the on-model frame beside the flat lay. Hem, sleeves and pockets are checked against the physical jacket before the listing goes up.

items.t: One standing scene for the launch
items.d: The boutique picks a single standing scene for the main photo of a new dress. Neckline, color, and how it fastens are compared with the garment on the rail before anyone posts it.

items.t: A back view from a second source
items.d: The label uses a photo of the back so the collar and rear seams can show. That second file is its own run, and the cost is shown before it starts.
The agency repeats upload, scene and download for each clothing client. People in the frames are generated. They are not hired models and not customers.
The square file goes on the product page, and the real size chart is added as text beside it. The photo does not invent measurements.
A puffer or coat is shown on a person instead of another hanger crop. Cuffs, pockets, and hem stay inside the uploaded photo so the result can be compared fairly.
They pick a generated person for the jacket instead of booking a model. Collar, hem, and color are checked against the garment.
The same on-model photo is paired with a spoken line in the language that country uses, without a second shoot.
They run the hanger photo again for another pose and another collection. Each run shows its credit cost first.
They check the hem against the real coat, trim the ad in the editor, and publish it to Instagram in one click.
